title: Tiny Cracks Help Solve a Mystery on Asteroid Bennu
summary:
In 2018, NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft reached an asteroid called Bennu. Scientists were surprised. Instead of smooth, sandy ground, Bennu was covered in huge boulders.

That was a puzzle. Earlier measurements showed Bennu's surface heats up and cools down fast, the way beach sand does. Big rocks usually hold heat and cool slowly, like concrete.

The spacecraft brought rock samples back to Earth. A team led by Andrew Ryan of the University of Arizona studied them. They found the rocks were full of tiny empty spaces and networks of cracks.

Scientists in Japan heated small spots on the samples with a laser to see how heat spread. At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, scientists sealed the rocks in airtight containers and used 3D X-ray scans to see inside without harming them. The results show that the size and inside structure of the rocks matter a lot. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications.
why_it_matters: Studying space rocks helps us learn how our solar system was made.
